summary: This EPA document (May 2012) lays out the strategic vision and guiding principles of the ENERGY STAR products labeling program, which aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by helping consumers and businesses identify the most energy-efficient product models that meet their needs. It describes the program design, the roles of EPA and the Department of Energy, six principles used to set new or revised product specifications, and the circumstances that prompt revising or sunsetting a specification, illustrated with examples. The note is cut off mid-sentence in the performance and quality section about lighting.
one_line: EPA's 2012 document defining the vision, design, and six guiding principles for setting and revising ENERGY STAR product efficiency specifications.
key_facts: The ENERGY STAR product labeling program aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by removing market barriers that deter consumers and businesses from identifying the financial and environmental benefits of the most energy-efficient product model that meets their needs.
EPA employs a set of six key principles when establishing or revising an ENERGY STAR product performance specification, and these principles are not applied as a strict checklist.

Experience has shown that it is typically possible to achieve the necessary balance among principles by selecting efficiency levels reflective of the top 25% of models available on the market when the specification goes into effect.

The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) leads the development of product testing procedures and metrics, performs verification testing and provides technical support in the development of ENERGY STAR product specifications.

Purchasers will recover their investment in increased energy efficiency within a reasonable period of time; ENERGY STAR specifications are set so that any cost differential at time of purchase is recovered through utility bill savings, generally between 2 and 5 years.
Since the first ENERGY STAR specification went into effect in 1992 for desktop computers and monitors, more than 150 revisions have been effective across more than 60 product categories.

Specifications for rapidly evolving products tend to be revised every two years, while specifications for more slowly advancing products are reviewed every three years or when market share reaches 35%.
As a general rule, product specifications will be reviewed for possible revision at least once every three years or when the market share of qualified products reaches about 35%.

In 2010, EPA analysis confirmed that the market share of ENERGY STAR qualified refrigerators had reached approximately 35% the preceding year, and EPA prioritized the refrigerator specification for review in 2011.

Although the market share of ENERGY STAR qualified televisions under Version 2.0 of the specification exceeded 90% for some time, the specification was not immediately revised because of challenges in addressing the "On Mode" power opportunity.

In 2007, EISA established new standards for the Energy Factor (EF) of dehumidifiers in various size classes, and EPA subsequently revised the ENERGY STAR dehumidifier specification to include levels more stringent than EISA.

In 2006, EPA revised the ENERGY STAR specification for oil furnaces from a minimum of 90% AFUE to 83% AFUE after builders in the Northeast U.S. reported a lack of available ENERGY STAR qualified equipment.

The ENERGY STAR specification for Programmable Thermostats is intended to save consumers 10-30% on the space heating and cooling portion of their energy bills, but field studies suggested lower savings, so EPA suspended the program while developing a usability metric.

The principle that a specification cannot be established if there is only one manufacturer of a product type, or one manufacturer holds a patent on the only efficiency technology, is stated explicitly, and EPA will not proceed in such cases.
